title: Unauthenticated users can lock out a known email address
description: The public sign-in Server Action accepts unauthenticated requests and forwards them to the backend. The backend counts attempts under a shared key derived only from the normalized email address, before checking whether the password is correct. After ten attempts in a 15-minute window, request 11 and all further sign-in attempts for that address receive HTTP 429 until the window expires. An attacker who knows a user's email can therefore repeatedly prevent that user from signing in; the attack does not grant access or affect other addresses.
root_cause: signIn in auth.service.ts applies a hard 15-minute login lockout keyed only by attacker-selectable email, allowing unauthenticated callers to deny sign-in to that address.
intended_behavior: Limit password guessing while allowing the legitimate account holder to continue signing in despite attempts made by another unauthenticated caller.

trace.description: The public login Server Action accepts an email and password without requiring an existing session, validates the form, then calls the backend login API.
The internal API login route passes the caller's email and password to AuthService.signIn; the public frontend action supplies the server-only internal API token.
The service normalizes the email and calls the shared rate limiter with the key login:<email>, limit 10, and a 900-second window before querying or verifying the account.
The rate limiter hashes only the supplied key, increments the shared database counter, and returns false after the limit is exceeded; AuthService then responds with HTTP 429.

conditions.description: The attacker must know or guess the target's email and submit 11 sign-in attempts within a 15-minute window.
No valid account or password is required; the sign-in action is public.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated visitor targeting a known user's email address.
payloads: Submit the public sign-in action with FormData fields email=owner@example.test and password=incorrect-value 11 times within 15 minutes.
instructions: Open the public login page or invoke its signIn Server Action as an unauthenticated visitor.
Submit the target email with an incorrect password ten times; each attempt reaches password verification and fails.
Submit the same email with an incorrect password once more; the backend rate limit rejects it with HTTP 429.
Have the legitimate account holder submit the correct password before the 15-minute window expires.
execution.expected_result: The legitimate login attempt is also rejected with HTTP 429 and the frontend displays the retry-in-15-minutes message, even though the attacker never authenticated.

remediation.strategy: Avoid an account-wide hard lockout that any unauthenticated caller can trigger. Use a trusted source-address throttle and progressive delay or challenge controls, with carefully bounded account-level monitoring that does not block the account holder solely because a third party made failed attempts.

code_changes.fixed_code: Apply login throttling using a trusted caller source plus account key, and do not return a persistent account-wide 429 solely because unauthenticated callers exhausted the email bucket.
Pass only a proxy-validated client address to the login throttling policy; do not trust caller-supplied forwarding headers directly.

likelihood.reason: The public login action is directly reachable and only 11 requests are needed, but the attacker must target a known email and external hosting controls were not reviewed.

impact.reason: The attacker can temporarily deny sign-in for one account for up to 15 minutes, but gains no access, cannot affect other emails, and can repeat only by making another short burst.

confidence.reason: The public Server Action, internal API call, email-only counter key, threshold, and 429 response were verified directly in source and independently reviewed. External WAF or hosting throttles were not available for inspection.

title: Public sign-up lets attackers claim an unverified email address
description: An unauthenticated visitor can submit an arbitrary, previously unused email address to the public sign-up action. The backend creates a user and session immediately without proving control of that email, and the frontend establishes a 30-day session before onboarding. The attacker can then create a shop and owner staff row tied to the claimed address. Because the email is unique and the app has no self-service recovery path, the legitimate holder cannot register with that address and may need operator intervention. This does not take over an existing account or expose pre-existing victim data; the impact is targeted account squatting, possible storefront impersonation, and registration denial.
root_cause: signUp in auth.service.ts creates a user session from an email address without verifying address ownership, allowing an attacker to claim an unused address and provision an owner shop under it.
intended_behavior: Let the rightful email holder create an application account and shop, while preventing an unrelated visitor from claiming that identity before ownership is established.

trace.description: The public sign-up Server Action accepts email and password form fields without requiring an existing session, then calls the backend sign-up API.
The guarded backend signup route accepts the email and password from the frontend action and passes them to AuthService; the frontend action supplies the server-held internal API token.
The service inserts the submitted, unverified email into the users table as the unique account identity.
After the signup action accepts the returned session, the authenticated onboarding action uses that account's user ID to create a shop.
The authenticated onboarding call inserts a shop and an owner staff record bound to the attacker-created user id.

conditions.description: The attacker must target a known email address whose rightful holder has not yet registered with the application.
No pre-existing account or password is required; public sign-up creates the attacker's own account using the claimed address.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated visitor who knows a business owner's email address before that owner registers with the service.
payloads: Submit the public sign-up action with FormData fields email=owner@business.example and password=AttackerChosenPassword123.
instructions: Open the public sign-up page while unauthenticated.
Submit an email address belonging to the intended business owner, provided that address has no existing application account, and choose an attacker-controlled password.
Use the resulting session to complete onboarding with a shop name and owner name associated with that business.
When the rightful holder attempts to sign up with the same address, observe the duplicate-account response; no email verification or self-service recovery is available in the reviewed flow.
execution.expected_result: The attacker controls an application account and owner shop under the submitted email, while the rightful holder is prevented from registering that email and may need manual operator recovery.

remediation.strategy: Require control of the email address before issuing an authenticated session or allowing shop onboarding. Store the account as pending until a short-lived, single-use verification token is redeemed; ensure the sign-in and shop-setup paths enforce verified status.

code_changes.fixed_code: Create unverified users in a pending state and do not return an authenticated session until a single-use email verification token has been redeemed.
After registration, prompt for email verification and prevent the account from reaching shop onboarding until the backend reports verified ownership.

likelihood.reason: Public sign-up requires only one request and business email addresses are often discoverable, but the attacker must act before the rightful holder registers and must target that specific address.

impact.reason: The attacker can reserve the account identity and create a shop appearing under that business email, blocking its rightful holder from registering; no existing account or data is taken over, and manual recovery may be possible.

confidence.reason: The signup, session, unique-address constraint, and shop-onboarding flow were verified directly and independently. Product documentation acknowledges missing email verification, so the intended identity policy is not explicit; the concrete registration-preemption behavior remains present.
